title: Japan weighs binding orders and penalties for the most powerful AI systems
excerpt: A government task force met on 11 November 2026 to discuss adding enforceable correction orders and penalties to Japan's AI law, limited to high-performance AI with serious risks.

sources.title: SBS News: Japan pushes to legally mandate AI safety measures and introduce penalties for violations
Newsquawk: Japanese government considering new penalties for AI service developers, Kyodo reports
TokenPost: Japan weighs binding orders and penalties for advanced AI firms
Future of Privacy Forum: Understanding Japan's AI Promotion Act

body_html:
Japan's government is considering giving its AI law real enforcement powers for the first time. A working-level government task force on AI legal and institutional issues met behind closed doors on 11 November 2026 and discussed requiring operators of high-performance AI to ensure safety, with penalties for those who ignore official orders. The plans were reported by Japan's Kyodo news agency and by the Mainichi Shimbun newspaper, as carried by SBS News and Newsquawk. No official government document has been published yet.

What Japan's AI law does today

Japan's main AI law, the Act on the Promotion of Research, Development and Utilization of AI-Related Technologies (often called the AI Promotion Act), was approved by parliament on 28 May 2025 and mostly took effect on 4 June 2025. According to an analysis by the Future of Privacy Forum, it lets the government collect information, study cases where people's rights are harmed, and give guidance to businesses. It contains no penalties. The only duty on companies is to "endeavor to cooperate" with government measures.

What is being discussed

According to the reports:

  • Correction orders: the government would be able to issue enforceable orders telling an AI operator to fix a problem.
  • Penalties: operators that ignore those orders, described as malicious or uncooperative, could be penalised. The reported examples are serious security or safety threats, such as a high-performance AI system becoming uncontrollable or being used for cyberattacks.
  • Narrow scope: penalties would apply only to high-performance AI with significant risks. Ordinary general-purpose AI would stay under existing laws and guidelines.
  • Timing: the government plans to outline the wider changes, including the content of a legal revision, by the end of 2026.

SBS reports that Anthropic, OpenAI Japan and the Japanese telecoms group NTT attended the meeting and shared their views and current safety work. The reports do not say what those companies said.

What is still unknown

Much is still open. The reports do not name the ministry that would enforce the rules, define "high-performance AI", or say what form or size the penalties would take. Which parts of the AI supply chain would be covered, from the developers of foundation models (large general-purpose models) to the services built on them, is still to be discussed. Newsquawk notes that this is an early, consideration-stage report, and that Japan has usually preferred consultation and voluntary rules before binding ones, so any bill could take time.

Why it matters for people staying in charge

The two risks named in the reports, an AI system that cannot be controlled and an AI system turned into a tool for attacks, sit at the centre of two Humasure Directives: D1 Always stoppable and D6 Secure and supported. A rule that lets a regulator order a fix, and act when the order is ignored, is about D9 Accountable: someone has to answer when something goes wrong.

Japan's move would bring it closer to places that already pair AI duties with enforcement, such as the European Union. It keeps the lighter, guidance-first approach for most AI and saves binding powers for the highest-risk systems. Humasure will follow the outline when it is published.
